title: Understanding Yourself Through Cognitive Behavioral Therapy
description: This article introduces the fundamentals of Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT) and demonstrates how core and intermediate beliefs shape automatic thoughts and emotions. Using the metaphor of an apple tree, it explains how internal frameworks influence our perception of events and our subsequent reactions. The provided examples illustrate why the same event can trigger vastly different emotions in different people.

texts: In today's world, filled with stress and uncertainty, psychological well-being is more important than ever.
Millions of people face challenges every day—ranging from mild discomfort and anxiety to more serious conditions such as depression, neurosis, post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD), and others.
These issues can significantly impact quality of life, making it difficult to enjoy daily moments, build meaningful relationships, or pursue personal goals.
If you are reading this and feel like something inside is preventing you from living life to the fullest—know that you are not alone; this is a natural part of the human experience.
Even the most successful and outwardly composed individuals deal with destructive mindsets and internal barriers.
Often, these roots go back to childhood, shaped by traumatic events or adverse circumstances.
<instagram>
It is important to remember: facing these difficulties does not make you "broken"—it is simply part of being human.
If you are ready for change, we invite you on a fascinating journey into the world of Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT).
This effective approach helps you understand yourself better and provides the tools to manage your thoughts and emotions.
In this chapter, we will begin by exploring the fundamental ideas of this method.
<q author='Rebecca Walker'>Our thoughts shape our perception, and our perception determines how we live.</q>
Whether your struggles feel minor or cause significant distress—from temporary low moods to long-standing symptoms—CBT can serve as a valuable resource.
Right now, we will present a simplified model of a key concept, which we will explore in greater depth in the following chapters.
In Cognitive Behavioral Therapy, the mind is conceptually described through three levels: core beliefs, intermediate beliefs (rules), and automatic thoughts.
The central idea of CBT is that our well-being and feelings depend on how we think.
<important>From this comes the core principle: when we notice and consciously adjust our thinking, life becomes more resilient and productive.</important>
This is a brief overview of the essence of CBT, but there are many important details ahead that we look forward to sharing with you.
To make this more visual, let's imagine an apple tree.
In this metaphor, the roots represent core beliefs: your fundamental assumptions about yourself, the world, and others.
They are formed by early experiences and are often unconscious. Examples include: "I am unlovable" or "The world is a dangerous place."
The trunk represents intermediate beliefs—the rules and assumptions that guide your day-to-day life.
They are built upon your core beliefs and direct your reactions. Examples include: "If I am not perfect, I won't be loved" or "To survive, I must always be on guard."
The canopy represents automatic thoughts: the rapid, spontaneous reactions to events.
These are like the fruit on the tree—they can be "healthy" or "rotten." Examples: "I'm late—I need to leave earlier next time" versus "I'm late—I am a failure."
Each of us has our own "tree," and we view every event through its unique lens.
This is why the exact same situation can trigger completely different emotions in different people—meaning is assigned through one's own beliefs.
This is how a wide spectrum of emotional responses is formed, even when facing externally identical events.
Let's look at an example. Two colleagues receive the same feedback at work:
Maria: since childhood, she has held the core belief "I am not good enough."

Her intermediate belief is: "To be valued, I must be flawless." Upon receiving criticism, she thinks: "I messed everything up; my boss is disappointed; I'm going to lose my job." The result: fear, anxiety, and exhaustion.
Kristina: she holds a different core belief—"I am capable of learning and growing."

Her intermediate belief is: "Criticism is an opportunity to improve." Upon hearing the feedback, she thinks: "My boss pointed out my weaknesses—this will help me improve my work." The result: calmness, motivation, and a readiness to correct mistakes.
So, the event is the same—feedback from a supervisor.
But the reactions are opposites due to the differences in their core and intermediate beliefs.
CBT helps you notice and change these beliefs so you can respond more constructively and maintain emotional balance.
<important>Because everyone has their own "tree model," identical situations are perceived differently.</important>
In response to these perceptions, automatic thoughts arise, which in turn influence emotions and behavior.
We will discuss the interconnectedness of thoughts, emotions, and behavior in much greater detail in the upcoming chapters.
We have only sketched the big picture in this chapter, so don't worry if you still have many questions; we will return to these ideas and break them down further.
We encourage you to approach this material with an open mind and a readiness to experiment. Put these techniques into practice—and let your life become fuller, more joyful, and more harmonious.
